content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Explain why plants need transport systems
Describe the structure and function of xylem and phloem
Explain the difference between transpiration and translocation
Describe the location of transport tissues in roots, stems, and leaves

Like animals, plants need to transport substances around their bodies. Water and minerals must travel from roots to leaves, while sugars produced in leaves must reach all cells. Plants use two types of transport tissue:
Why Do Plants Need Transport Systems?
Large plants cannot rely on diffusion alone:
Diffusion is too slow over large distances
Leaves need water from roots (may be metres away)
Living cells (but no nucleus when mature)
Connected to sieve tube by plasmodesmata

content.text: Xylem on inside, phloem on outside in each bundle.
Xylem on upper side, phloem below
Growing tips, roots, storage organs, fruits
Where sugars are made or stored (mature leaves)
Where sugars are used or stored (roots, fruits, growing tips)
Xylem and phloem are the same thing
They're different tissues with different structures and functions
Phloem transports to wherever sugars are needed (up or down)
Mature xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes
Plants have a heart to pump water
Water movement is passive, driven by transpiration
Loss of water vapour from leaves
Plants need transport systems because diffusion is too slow
Xylem transports water and minerals upward (passive)
Phloem transports sugars in both directions (active)
Xylem: dead cells, lignified, no end walls
Phloem: living cells, sieve plates, companion cells
In stems: vascular bundles in a ring, xylem inside
In roots: xylem in centre, star-shaped
Transpiration = water movement; translocation = sugar movement
